name: More Is Different
aliases: The autonomy of the special sciences
statement: Assemble enough parts and entirely new laws emerge that knowing the pieces alone would never let you predict.
meaning: More Is Different is the principle, argued by the physicist Philip W. Anderson in a 1972 essay, that being able to reduce everything to a few fundamental laws does not imply being able to start from those laws and reconstruct the world. Anderson accepted reductionism, that all matter obeys the same underlying laws, but rejected what he called the constructionist inference that follows from it. At each new level of scale and complexity, he held, genuinely new properties and organising principles appear that are not a simple extrapolation of the level below, so more of the same components can behave in a way that is not merely larger but qualitatively different.
mechanism: The argument turns on scale and complexity defeating construction. A large aggregate of particles can settle into a collective state whose symmetry is lower than that of the laws governing it, a phenomenon Anderson calls broken symmetry, visible in crystals, magnets, and superconductors, and out of that broken symmetry come new, level-specific regularities. He lays out a rough hierarchy of the sciences, from particle physics up through chemistry, molecular biology, and on to psychology and the social sciences, and argues that each level obeys its own fundamental laws that cannot in practice be derived from the level beneath, so psychology is not applied biology, nor biology applied chemistry.

examples.text: A crystal or a magnet has a definite orientation its underlying laws do not single out; the many-body state breaks the symmetry, producing rigidity and order that no single particle possesses.
Anderson's own gloss that each science rests on but is not reducible to the one below, so chemistry is not merely applied particle physics, and each level needs its own concepts.
His summary that the whole becomes not only more than but very different from the sum of its parts, stated in the context of broken symmetry rather than as a loose slogan.

variants.name: Reductionism versus constructionism
variants.text: Anderson's key distinction: he grants that everything reduces to fundamental laws but denies that mastery of those laws lets you build the higher levels back up.

variants.name: Weinberg's two cheers
variants.text: Steven Weinberg's rejoinder distinguishing grand reductionism, that all principles trace to a few universal laws, which he defends, from petty reductionism, that big things are nothing but their parts, which he too rejects.

whyItMatters: More Is Different became the charter statement for emergence and for the intellectual independence of the special sciences, defending condensed-matter and higher-level fields against being dismissed as mere applications of fundamental physics. It reframed the reductionism debate by separating the truth of reductionism from the false hope of constructionism, and it became a philosophical touchstone for complexity science, a field Anderson later helped launch as a co-founder of the Santa Fe Institute. Few short essays have so shaped how scientists think about the relation between levels of nature.

working.text: grant that higher levels obey the same fundamental laws, while denying that those laws let you predict or rebuild the higher levels.

working.lead: Look for new laws at each level
working.text: expect qualitatively new organising principles to appear as complexity grows, not just more of the lower-level behaviour.
treat chemistry, biology, and psychology as autonomous rather than as applied physics awaiting derivation.

limits: The essay is a philosophical argument, not an empirical law, and its interpretation is contested. Anderson supports at most the weaker, epistemological reading, that we cannot in practice derive or predict higher levels, and whether it implies strong, ontological emergence, genuinely new causal powers, is disputed. Reductionists such as Steven Weinberg reply that emergent-level laws still hold because of, and are constrained by, the deeper laws, so higher levels are reducible in principle even if not in practice. The line between in-principle and in-practice reduction is exactly where the debate lives, and More Is Different does not settle it so much as open it.
misreadings: Anderson did not reject reductionism; he accepted fundamental laws and rejected only the constructionist leap from them. Notably, the essay never actually uses the word emergence, though it is read as the founding statement of the idea, so crediting it with coining the term is a mistake. The famous line is specifically that the whole becomes not only more than but very different from the sum of its parts, tied to broken symmetry, not the vaguer, older Aristotelian saying that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. And it is a disciplinary defence of higher-level physics, not an anti-science manifesto.
origin: From Philip W. Anderson's essay 'More Is Different: Broken symmetry and the nature of the hierarchical structure of science', published in Science in August 1972 and based on a 1967 lecture; Anderson won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1977.

sources.text: Anderson, 'More Is Different,' Science 177(4047):393-396 (1972). — the constructionist critique, broken symmetry, and the hierarchy of the sciences.
